page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: Molality (m) is the number of moles of
solute present in one kilogram of SOLVENT.
steps.why: Molality is measured against the mass of solvent, not against the volume of solution, so both quantities in it are masses. That is exactly why it is the concentration term used in the boiling point and freezing point equations, where the temperature of the solution is being changed on purpose.
common_mistakes: Writing "one kilogram of solution". Molality is per kilogram of SOLVENT.
Mixing up the symbols m and M. Small m is molality, capital M is molarity.
steps.memory_tip: Molality is per kilogram of solvent. Mass on both sides, so no volume anywhere in it.
steps.margin_note: The word SOLVENT is the marked word in this line. Underline it.

steps.label: The formula and the unit
lines: w = mass of solute in gram
GMW = gram molecular weight of the solute
W = mass of the solvent in gram
Molality does not change with temperature,
because a mass does not change with
steps.why: The 1000 converts the mass of solvent from gram to kilogram, so the formula is the definition written for quantities that are weighed. Since only masses appear, heating the solution changes nothing in the formula, and this is why ΔTb = Kb m and ΔTf = Kf m are written in molality and not in molarity.
common_mistakes: Putting the mass of the SOLUTION in the denominator. In a 10% w/w solution that mistake uses 100 g in place of 90 g.
Writing the unit as mol L⁻¹. Molality has no volume, so its unit is mol kg⁻¹.
steps.memory_tip: Molality is all mass, so temperature cannot change it.
steps.margin_note: Write the unit mol kg⁻¹ and the temperature line. Together they are usually the second half of this mark.

insider_note: The elevation and depression formulas both use molality, never molarity. Saying why in one line, that a mass does not change when the solution is heated or cooled, is what a full answer adds.
